common_name: Naomi Japanese Forest Grass (Red-Tinted Fall Foliage Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Set divisions out in spring once frost danger has passed, siting them in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a compact sport of 'Aureola', it stays smaller and colors earlier in fall.

directions: Plant in humus-rich soil sheltered from afternoon sun, where the gold-and-green variegated blades can develop their signature red-purple flush through summer into fall. Keep the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged, mulching to conserve moisture in warmer climates. Clumps expand slowly by rhizome, so division is rarely needed more than once every several years. Cut back dead foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: SunFlare Japanese Forest Grass (Compact Gold Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring as new blades emerge, choosing a site with rich, well-drained soil and shelter from hot midday sun; this dwarf sport of 'All Gold' forms a tighter, more compact mound than the species.

directions: Grow in bright, dappled shade or morning sun in soil enriched with organic matter, watering regularly so the shallow roots never dry out. Chartreuse-to-golden blades pick up crimson highlights through summer and burnt-orange tones in fall, deepening further as clumps mature past their second year. Because it increases slowly from dense rhizomes, this grass rarely needs dividing and works well in containers or as a small-scale edging plant. Remove old foliage in late winter before fresh growth resumes.

planting.note: Set rooted divisions or nursery plants out in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; because its pale gold-and-cream leaves scorch easily, avoid sites with strong afternoon sun.

directions: Site this slow-spreading bugleweed where bright shade shields its cream-and-gold foliage from harsh midday sun, since its light coloration is more prone to leaf burn than green- or bronze-leaved forms. Spring flushes bring a pink blush to the variegation before short spikes of blue flowers appear above the mat. Keep soil evenly moist and well-drained, and thin congested patches after a few seasons to maintain vigor. Its slower spread makes it a good fit for small-scale groundcover plantings and mixed containers rather than large-scale erosion control.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of Extension

common_name: Cordial Canary Bugleweed (Feathered Friends Series Chartreuse Ajuga)

planting.note: Plant divisions or starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; part of the Feathered Friends series bred for bright, non-fading foliage color, it spreads readily to knit into a dense mat.

directions: This chartreuse-leaved bugleweed forms a dense, low groundcover that brightens shaded beds and woodland edges beneath trees and shrubs. Short spikes of blue flowers rise above the foliage in late spring, drawing bees and other pollinators. Provide consistent moisture and good drainage, since soggy winter soil is more damaging to this ground-hugging perennial than cold alone. Trim back any winter-damaged leaves in early spring to make way for fresh chartreuse growth.
